question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below
Amalgamate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Dismantle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Amalgamate" means to combine or unite two or more things (especially organizations or metals) into one. (मिलाना/एकीकृत करना)
◦ Example: The two companies decided to amalgamate their operations to cut costs.

• Its antonym must convey the opposite idea — to take apart, separate, or break up something that was combined.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Integrate" (एकीकृत करना): To combine one thing with another so that they become a whole — this is a synonym, not an antonym, of amalgamate.

• Option 2: "Combine" (मिलाना): To join or merge together — again a synonym of amalgamate.

• Option 4: "Coalesce" (एक साथ मिलना): To come together and form one mass or whole — also a synonym, describing separate elements uniting.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of amalgamate: merge, fuse, blend, consolidate, unify.

• Other antonyms of amalgamate: separate, divide, split, disunite, segregate.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Trnuk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Trunk" — referring to the main stem of a tree, the long nose of an elephant, the main body of a structure, or a large box/suitcase used for storage or travel.
◦ Example: The elephant used its trunk to lift the log.

• In the given option, the letters "u" and "n" have been wrongly interchanged/reordered, producing the misspelling "Trnuk" instead of "Trunk".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Blade" — correctly spelt; the flat cutting part of a knife or a leaf-like structure.

• Option 3: "Mentor" — correctly spelt; an experienced person who guides or trains a less experienced one.

• Option 4: "Dinner" — correctly spelt; the main evening meal.

NOTE

• Always double-check the internal letter order in short, common nouns — SSC frequently tests jumbled-letter misspellings like "Trnuk", "Freind" (for Friend) or "Recieve" (for Receive).

• Remember the rule "i before e except after c" for words like receive, deceive, and believe.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Nark
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Irritate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Nark" (used informally, especially in British English) means to annoy, irritate, or provoke someone. (चिढ़ाना/नाराज़ करना)
◦ Example: It really narks me when people talk loudly during a film.

• As a noun, "nark" can also mean a police informer, but as tested here (matching the given options) its closest meaning is "to irritate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reassure" (आश्वस्त करना): To restore someone's confidence; to remove their doubts — nearly opposite in feel to nark.

• Option 3: "Solace" (सांत्वना): Comfort or consolation in a time of distress — the opposite of irritation.

• Option 4: "Obligation" (बाध्यता): A duty or commitment to do something — unrelated in meaning to nark.

NOTE

• Other informal words meaning "to irritate": rile, needle, vex, peeve, exasperate.

• Do not confuse "nark" (to irritate/an informer) with "narc" (a narcotics agent) — the two are pronounced alike but spelt differently.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Have people rolling in the aisles
option_1: To use false promises to pull people on one's side
option_3: To have a dispute with someone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Make an audience laugh uncontrollably.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Have people rolling in the aisles" means to make an audience laugh so hard that they double over with laughter, as if rolling about in the aisles of a theatre. (दर्शकों को खूब हंसाना)
◦ Example: The stand-up comedian had people rolling in the aisles within the first five minutes of his act.

• The image behind the idiom is of theatre-goers laughing so uncontrollably that they slip out of their seats into the aisles.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To use false promises to pull people on one's side: Describes deceitful persuasion, unrelated to laughter — this matches idioms like "to butter someone up" or "to sweet-talk".

• Option 3: To have a dispute with someone: Describes conflict, matching idioms like "to lock horns" or "to be at loggerheads".

• Option 4: Willing to do something immediately: Describes readiness, matching idioms like "raring to go" or "to jump at the chance".

NOTE

• Other laughter-related idioms often asked in SSC: "to split one's sides" (to laugh very hard) and "to be in stitches" (to laugh uncontrollably).

• Do not confuse with "to bring the house down", which similarly means to receive a huge, enthusiastic (often laughing/applauding) response from an audience.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A religions war
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Crusade.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Crusade" means a war or military expedition undertaken in the name of religion, originally referring to the medieval Christian expeditions to recover the Holy Land. (धर्म युद्ध)
◦ Example: The Crusades were a series of religious wars fought between Christians and Muslims in the Middle Ages.

• The word is also used figuratively for any vigorous campaign for a cause, but its primary/literal sense — a religious war — is what is tested here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Inscription" (शिलालेख): Words engraved or carved on a surface such as a stone, coin, or monument.

• Option 2: "Colonialism" (उपनिवेशवाद): The policy of acquiring and maintaining colonies, i.e., political/economic control over another country.

• Option 3: "Colloquial" (बोलचाल की भाषा): An adjective describing language used in ordinary/familiar conversation rather than formal writing.

NOTE

• Other one-word substitutions for types of conflict: "Civil war" (war between citizens of the same country), "Guerrilla warfare" (irregular fighting by small groups), and "Mutiny" (open rebellion against authority, especially in the armed forces).

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: The cursor must be plased at the strat of the line.
option_2: The cursor must be placed at the start of the line.
option_3: The cursor must be plased at the start of the line.
option_4: The cursur must be placed at the start of the line.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The cursor must be placed at the start of the line.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly spelt sentence must use "cursor" (not "cursur"), "placed" (not "plased"), and "start" (not "strat").

• Option 2 contains all three words spelt correctly: "cursor", "placed", and "start".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Contains two misspellings — "plased" (should be "placed") and "strat" (should be "start").

• Option 3: Contains one misspelling — "plased" (should be "placed").

• Option 4: Contains one misspelling — "cursur" (should be "cursor").

NOTE

• Watch for letter-order errors (e.g., "strat"/"start", "cursur"/"cursor") and dropped/added letters (e.g., "plased"/"placed") — these are the two commonest misspelling patterns SSC uses in "choose the correct/incorrect spelling" questions.

• Practice writing out commonly confused technical words like cursor, keyboard, and monitor to avoid such slips.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
In the flesh
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In bodily form.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "In the flesh" means in person; physically present, as opposed to on screen, in a photograph, or described in words. (साक्षात/शरीर सहित प्रत्यक्ष रूप से)
◦ Example: I have seen the actor in movies many times, but never in the flesh.

• The phrase emphasizes actual physical presence of a person, i.e., their real bodily form, in front of you.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To be near death: Matches idioms like "to be at death's door" or "to have one foot in the grave", not "in the flesh".

• Option 2: To talk: Matches idioms like "to have a chinwag" or "to chew the fat", unrelated to "in the flesh".

• Option 4: To get a tattoo: Not an idiomatic meaning of "in the flesh" at all; getting a tattoo has no standard idiom involving "flesh".

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "in person": "face to face" and "in person" itself.

• Do not confuse "in the flesh" with "flesh and blood", which refers to one's own close blood relatives, or with "to put flesh on the bones (of something)", which means to add detail to a plan or idea.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. the shape of an egg has been highly regarded for its evolution
Q. the body in the most efficient way, not roll away once laid, is structurally
R. as large enough to incubate an embryo, small enough to exit
S. sound enough to bear weight and be the beginning of life for so many species
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. PRQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) questions, the parts must be joined so that the sentence reads as one grammatically complete and logically coherent unit.

• P — "the shape of an egg has been highly regarded for its evolution" — introduces the subject, so it must come first.

• R — "as large enough to incubate an embryo, small enough to exit" — naturally follows "evolution", explaining the purpose behind the egg's shape.

• Q — "the body in the most efficient way, not roll away once laid, is structurally" — completes the idea of exiting "the body" and leads into the final quality ("structurally sound").

• S — "sound enough to bear weight and be the beginning of life for so many species" — completes "structurally sound enough", giving the sentence its logical ending.

• Joining them in the order P-R-Q-S gives: "The shape of an egg has been highly regarded for its evolution as large enough to incubate an embryo, small enough to exit the body in the most efficient way, not roll away once laid, is structurally sound enough to bear weight and be the beginning of life for so many species." — a single coherent sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (QPRS) is incorrect because it begins with "the body", which has no subject/context established yet — "the body" of what is unclear without P coming first.

• Option 3 (PSQR) is incorrect because after P it jumps straight to S ("sound enough to bear weight..."), making "sound" appear before the word "structurally" that it must follow, breaking the sense.

• Option 4 (SPQR) is incorrect because it starts with S, a concluding clause, which cannot logically open the sentence.

NOTE

• In such single-sentence four-part rearrangements, always look first for the part that can stand as a grammatically complete opening clause (usually containing the main subject and verb) — that part starts the sentence.

• Then match linking words/phrases (pronouns, articles like "the", and participial phrases) across the parts to chain them correctly.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
He said, “I will go to Indonesia tomorrow”.
option_1: He said that he would go to Indonesia tomorrow.
option_2: He said that he would go to Indonesia the next day.
option_3: He said that he would be going to Indonesia the next day.
option_4: He said he would go to Indonesia by tomorrow.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He said that he would go to Indonesia the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence, "He said, 'I will go to Indonesia tomorrow'", is in the Simple Future Tense within direct speech.

• Rule — reporting future tense (will/shall): In indirect speech, "will/shall" changes to "would", and the pronoun "I" changes according to the subject of the reporting verb (here, "he").

• Rule — time expressions: Since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, time words shift as follows: "tomorrow" → "the next day" (or "the following day").

• Applying these rules: I → he; will go → would go; tomorrow → the next day.

• Result: He said that he would go to Indonesia the next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it retains "tomorrow" instead of correctly changing it to "the next day", which is required since the reporting verb is in the past tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it wrongly uses the continuous form "would be going" instead of the simple form "would go", which changes the meaning/tense unnecessarily.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it uses the odd phrase "by tomorrow" and drops the conjunction "that"; it also fails to change "tomorrow" appropriately.

NOTE

• Common time-word changes in narration: today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day/the day before; now → then; here → there; this → that.

• Modal changes: will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to/must (no change if a permanent truth).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
A disconsolate Arjun ______ his way back down the mountain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. makes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires the fixed collocation "make one's way", which means to go or travel, often with some effort or in a particular direction.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: The subject "A disconsolate Arjun" is third person singular, so in the Simple Present Tense the verb must take the -s/-es form: "makes".

• Applying the collocation and the agreement rule: "A disconsolate Arjun makes his way back down the mountain" is the grammatically and idiomatically correct sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "absconds" means to run away secretly, usually to escape from custody or duty — it does not collocate with "his way" and changes the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "elopes" means to run away secretly, especially to marry without parental consent — inappropriate in this context and does not take "his way" as an object.

• Option 3: "deserts" means to abandon a person, place, or post disloyally — it also does not fit the fixed phrase "—— one's way".

NOTE

• Other common "make" collocations tested by SSC: make a decision, make an effort, make progress, make amends, make a mistake, make sense (of something).

• Do not confuse "deserts" (verb, to abandon) with "desserts" (sweet dish) or with the noun "deserts" (as in "just deserts", meaning what one rightfully deserves).

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A slight fault that can be forgiven
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Venial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Venial" means (of a sin, fault, or offence) slight and pardonable; excusable. (क्षम्य/मामूली)
◦ Example: Forgetting to reply to an email is a venial lapse, not a serious offence.

• The word is most often used in the phrase "venial sin", as opposed to a "mortal/cardinal sin", which is grave and unforgivable.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Referral" (संदर्भ/सिफ़ारिश): The act of directing someone to another person or place for information, help, or treatment.

• Option 2: "Libertine" (स्वच्छंद व्यक्ति): A person who behaves without moral restraint, especially in sexual matters.

• Option 4: "Libel" (मानहानि): A published false statement that damages a person's reputation.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Venial" with "Venal", which means open to bribery or corruption (a completely different, more serious fault).

• Other one-word substitutes for types of faults/offences: "Peccadillo" (a small, relatively unimportant offence) and "Cardinal sin" (a very serious fault/error).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
If you doesn't have a doctor, contact your public health authority.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. If you doesn't have.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "do/does": The auxiliary "does" (and its negative "doesn't") is used only with third-person singular subjects (he/she/it, or a singular noun). The pronoun "you" always takes "do/don't", regardless of whether it refers to one person or many.

• In the given sentence, "If you doesn't have a doctor..." wrongly pairs the second-person pronoun "you" with the third-person auxiliary "doesn't".

• The corrected sentence should read: "If you don't have a doctor, contact your public health authority."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "your public health authority." is grammatically correct as it stands and contains no error.

• Option 2: "a doctor, contact" is grammatically correct; "contact" is the correct imperative verb form needed here.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect as an answer because an error does exist, in the segment identified in Option 4.

NOTE

• Remember: I/you/we/they → do/don't; he/she/it (singular) → does/doesn't.

• This is one of the most frequently tested agreement errors in SSC error-spotting questions — always check that "do/does", "has/have", and "is/are/am" match their subjects in person and number.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Remedy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Panacea.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Remedy" means a medicine or treatment for a disease or injury, or more generally a means of counteracting or solving a problem. (उपाय/इलाज)

• A "Panacea" means a solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases; a cure-all, making it the closest match among the given options to "remedy". (रामबाण इलाज)
◦ Example: Exercise is often called a panacea for many lifestyle diseases.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Parochial" (संकीर्ण): Having a narrow, limited, or provincial outlook; concerned only with a small area or one's own restricted interests.

• Option 2: "Tablet" (गोली): A small, solid, flat piece of medicine — this is a form a remedy may take, not a synonym for the concept of "remedy" itself.

• Option 3: "Plagiarism" (साहित्यिक चोरी): The practice of taking someone else's work or ideas and passing them off as one's own.

NOTE

• Other words close to "remedy": cure, antidote, solution, corrective, therapy.

• Do not confuse "Panacea" (a cure for everything) with "Placebo" (a substance with no therapeutic effect, given to satisfy a patient) — the two are often confused in vocabulary sections.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
I believe that we are ________ responsible for our choices.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. solely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Solely" means only, exclusively, entirely — and it collocates naturally with the adjective "responsible" in the fixed phrase "solely responsible (for)", meaning having the entire, undivided responsibility for something.

• The sentence needs an adverb that fits between "are" and "responsible" and makes logical sense: "we are solely responsible for our choices" means we alone bear responsibility for them, with no one else to share the blame.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "profusely" means abundantly or in large amounts (e.g., "bleeding profusely", "apologised profusely") — it does not collocate with "responsible".

• Option 2: "durably" means in a way that lasts a long time without breaking down — irrelevant to the idea of responsibility.

• Option 4: "ordinarily" means usually or normally — while grammatically possible, it does not convey the intended sense of exclusive/total responsibility as precisely and naturally as "solely" does.

NOTE

• Other common adverb + "responsible" collocations: directly responsible, jointly responsible, personally responsible, ultimately responsible.

• "Solely" is often confused in spelling with "soley"/"solly" — remember it is formed from "sole" (only) + "-ly".

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
She told me to wait here.
option_1: I was told to wait here by her.
option_2: I was told to wait there by her.
option_3: I was told to waited here by her.
option_4: I am told to wait here by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I was told to wait here by her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "She told me to wait here" uses the pattern Subject + told + Object + to + V1 (infinitive), a common structure for reported instructions.

• Rule — Passive of "told + object + infinitive": Object of the active sentence → Subject of the passive; the verb "told" becomes "was/were told"; the infinitive ("to wait") and any adverb/place phrase are retained as they are; the original subject becomes the agent with "by".

• Applying the rule: "me" → "I"; "told" → "was told" (singular subject "I"); "to wait here" stays unchanged; "she" → "by her".

• Passive: I was told to wait here by her.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "there" wrongly replaces "here"; the place adverb must remain exactly as in the active sentence — "here", not "there".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "to waited" is not a valid infinitive form; after "to", only the base form of the verb ("wait") can be used, never the past form.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "am told" wrongly uses the Present Tense; since the active sentence is in the Past Tense ("told"), the passive must also be in the Past Tense ("was told").

NOTE

• The structure "Subject + verb (ask/tell/order) + Object + to + V1" is passivised as "Object + is/was + verb (asked/told/ordered) + to + V1 + by + Subject" — this pattern is very frequently tested in SSC.

• Common verbs following this pattern: ask, tell, order, request, advise, allow, permit, invite, persuade.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The shelf is too highest for me to reach.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. too high.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "too" + Adjective: The word "too" (meaning "excessively") is always followed by the positive/base degree of the adjective, never the comparative or superlative degree.

• In the given sentence, "too highest" wrongly combines "too" with the superlative form "highest", which is grammatically incorrect.

• The correct form is: "The shelf is too high for me to reach."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "too highly" is incorrect because "highly" is an adverb (used with verbs like "regard" or "praise"), not an adjective describing the shelf's physical height.

• Option 2: "more higher" is incorrect because it is a double comparative — "more" should never be used together with a word that already ends in "-er" (the comparative suffix); it should be simply "higher".

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original phrase "too highest" is clearly ungrammatical and needs correction.

NOTE

• "too" + base adjective: too big, too small, too tall, too high, too expensive.

• Never combine "more"/"most" with an "-er"/"-est" form (avoid "more better", "most best", "more higher") — this is one of the commonest SSC error types.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
They weren't allows to take their dog into the store.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. allowed to take.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with "They weren't", a Past Tense negative auxiliary ("were" + "not"), which requires the past participle (V3) form of the main verb to form the passive-style construction that follows.

• Rule — "be + past participle + to + V1": After "weren't" (were not), the verb must be in its past participle form: "allowed", followed by the infinitive "to take".

• Corrected sentence: "They weren't allowed to take their dog into the store."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "allowed to took" is incorrect because after the infinitive marker "to", only the base form of the verb ("take") can follow, never the past form ("took").

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because "allows to take" does not agree in tense with the past auxiliary "weren't"; "allows" is a present-tense form and cannot follow "were".

• Option 3: "allow to take" is incorrect because the base form "allow" cannot directly follow "weren't"; the passive construction requires the past participle "allowed".

NOTE

• Structure: Subject + was/were (+not) + past participle + to + V1 (e.g., "He was allowed to leave", "They were asked to wait").

• Common confusion: after "to" (infinitive marker), always use the base verb form, e.g., "to take", "to go", "to see" — never "to took", "to went", "to saw".

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.
The palace was in turmoil because Sikhandi (had return.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. had returned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes two past events: the palace being in turmoil (past event) and the reason behind it — Sikhandi's action, which happened before that turmoil. When one past action occurs before another past action, the earlier one is expressed using the Past Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense: Subject + had + V3 (past participle).

• Here, "return" in its past participle form is "returned", so the bracketed segment must read "had returned": "The palace was in turmoil because Sikhandi had returned."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "No correction required" is incorrect because "had return" is not a valid verb form — "had" must be followed by a past participle (V3), not the base form "return".

• Option 3: "have turned" is incorrect both in tense (Present Perfect, not Past Perfect) and in meaning ("turned" is a different verb from "returned").

• Option 4: "was return" is incorrect because "was" must be followed by a present participle ("returning") to form the past continuous, or the sentence needs "had returned" for the past perfect — "was return" is not a valid verb form at all.

NOTE

• The Past Perfect Tense is used for the earlier of two past actions — remember: "the action that happened first gets 'had + V3'".

• Common trigger words for the Past Perfect: "because", "after", "before", "already", "by the time", "when" (with two past clauses).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The Event Horizon Telescope can help scientists analyse the shapes and behaviours of event horizons.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The Event Horizon Telescope can help scientists analyse the shapes and behaviours of event horizons" is grammatically correct in every part.

• Subject-verb agreement: The singular subject "The Event Horizon Telescope" correctly takes the modal "can", which does not change with number/person.

• Verb pattern: "help + object + base verb (analyse)" is a correctly used structure ("help someone (to) do something").

• Parallel structure: "the shapes and behaviours of event horizons" correctly uses two plural nouns joined by "and", both governed by "of event horizons".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "and behaviours of event horizons." contains no grammatical fault — the plural noun "behaviours" and prepositional phrase are correctly formed.

• Option 3: "The Event Horizon Telescope can" is correct — a singular subject with the invariant modal verb "can".

• Option 4: "help scientists analyse the shapes" is correct — this is the standard "help + object + bare infinitive" pattern ("to" is optional after "help").

NOTE

• After the verb "help", both the bare infinitive ("help him do") and the to-infinitive ("help him to do") are grammatically acceptable in modern English.

• Always check for hidden agreement or tense errors before assuming a sentence has a mistake — SSC includes genuinely error-free sentences to test this skill specifically.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Nascence
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Incipience.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Nascence" (also spelt "nascency") means the process of being born or coming into existence; a beginning. (उत्पत्ति/जन्म)

• "Incipience" means the beginning or initial stage of something's existence, making it a close synonym of "nascence". (आरंभ/प्रारंभिक अवस्था)
◦ Example: The project is still in its incipience, with much work left to be done.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Cessation" (समाप्ति): The fact or process of ending or being brought to an end — an antonym, not a synonym, of nascence.

• Option 3: "Omega" (अंत): The last letter of the Greek alphabet, used figuratively to mean "the end" of something — again roughly opposite in sense to a beginning.

• Option 4: "Acrimonious" (कटु): An adjective meaning bitter and angry in tone, typically describing a dispute or argument — unrelated in meaning to nascence.

NOTE

• Words related to "beginning": genesis, inception, onset, dawn, outset.

• Words related to "end" (often confused as distractors in such questions): cessation, culmination, termination, finale, omega.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.

Comprehension: In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie’s younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie’s been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she’s steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap’n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. refused.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard)."

• The idiom "to put one's foot down" means to take a firm stand or to insist on something, often against pressure or the usual expectation.

• The contrast word "but" and the phrase "for once" signal that the speaker is doing something unusual — resisting the pull toward the "Best School" (Harvard) and sticking with her choice (Yale). The verb that best fits this firm, resistant stance, followed by "to apply", is "refused".

• Reading it in context: she took a firm stand and refused to apply to Harvard, choosing to stay with Yale instead.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "rejoiced" means to feel or show great joy — it does not logically pair with "to apply", and there is no indication of joy in the passage's tone.

• Option 3: "dwelled" means to live somewhere, or (as "dwelled on") to think or talk about something at length — it does not fit the structure "______ to apply".

• Option 4: "levelled" means to make flat or even, or (informally) to be honest with someone ("level with") — it does not fit this context or the following infinitive "to apply".

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read at least one full sentence around the blank (and note contrast words like "but", "however", "although") to correctly gauge the tone and logical direction before choosing an option.

• The idiom "put one's foot down" is a frequently tested phrase in SSC vocabulary/cloze sections, meaning to assert oneself firmly.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.

Comprehension: In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie’s younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie’s been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she’s steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap’n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. being.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "The idea of (2) ______ Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far."

• Rule — verb form after a preposition: A preposition (here, "of") must always be followed by a noun, pronoun, or a gerund (verb + -ing) — never by a base form, an infinitive, or a participle like "been"/"be".

• The gerund "being" correctly follows the preposition "of" and combines with the noun phrase that follows to form the sense "the idea of being [someone]'s younger brother".

• Corrected: "The idea of being Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "been" is the past participle form, used after "have/has/had" (e.g., "has been"), not directly after a preposition.

• Option 2: "having been" is a perfect gerund/participle form that is grammatically heavier and unnecessary here; it does not fit as naturally as the simple gerund "being" in this context.

• Option 3: "be" is the base form of the verb and cannot directly follow a preposition; it needs "to be" (infinitive) or "being" (gerund).

NOTE

• Rule to remember: preposition + gerund (V-ing), e.g., "good at swimming", "interested in learning", "the idea of being".

• Do not confuse this rule with "to + base verb" (infinitive), which follows many verbs and adjectives but never directly follows a preposition (except "about to").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.

Comprehension: In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie’s younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie’s been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she’s steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap’n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. who.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended."

• Rule — relative/interrogative pronoun "who": "Who" is used as the subject of a clause when referring to a person, and it is also the pronoun used in the idiomatic expression "who knows", meaning "nobody can be certain".

• Here, the blank is immediately followed by the verb "knows", so the pronoun must function as the subject of "knows" — this is the job of "who", not "whom" (object form), "which" (used for things), or "whose" (possessive form).

• Corrected: "Besides, who knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "whose" is a possessive pronoun (e.g., "whose book is this") and cannot act as the subject of "knows".

• Option 2: "which" is used to refer to things or animals, not people, so it cannot be the subject of "knows" in a sentence about who is aware of something.

• Option 4: "whom" is the object form of "who", used when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition (e.g., "whom did you see"), not when it is the subject of the following verb.

NOTE

• Quick check: if the pronoun is followed directly by a verb (as its subject), use "who"; if it is followed by a subject + verb (i.e., it is the object), use "whom" (e.g., "the man whom I met").

• "Who knows" is a common idiomatic expression meaning it is uncertain or impossible to say for sure.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.

Comprehension: In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie’s younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie’s been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she’s steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap’n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen."

• Rule — subject pronoun: Since "My mom and ______" together form the subject of the verb "are", the pronoun in the blank must be in the subjective/nominative case. The subjective form of the first-person singular pronoun is "I" (not the objective form "me").

• Corrected: "My mom and I are in the kitchen."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "me" is the objective case of the first-person pronoun, used when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition (e.g., "She saw me"), not when it is part of the subject.

• Option 3: "am" is a verb form (the first-person singular form of "to be"), not a pronoun, so it cannot fill a noun/pronoun slot alongside "My mom and".

• Option 4: "myself" is a reflexive pronoun, used when the subject and object of the same clause refer to the same person (e.g., "I hurt myself"), and is not appropriate as a simple subject here.

NOTE

• A simple test: remove "My mom and" from the sentence and see which pronoun sounds correct alone — "I am in the kitchen" (correct) versus "Me am in the kitchen" (incorrect) — confirming that "I" is the subject form needed.

• Common SSC trap: many candidates default to "me" in compound subjects ("my friend and me") out of habit from spoken English, but the subjective case ("I") is grammatically required when the pronoun is part of the subject.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. writing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook."

• Rule — parallel structure: The blank is joined by "and" to the earlier verb "am having", so the missing verb must also be in the present continuous (-ing) form to remain parallel: "I am having... and (5) ______ing...".

• Contextually, a Moleskine notebook is used for jotting down notes or journal entries, so the action performed "in" a notebook that fits best is "writing".

• Corrected: "I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch... and writing in my Moleskine notebook."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sieving" means passing something through a sieve to separate coarse and fine particles — an odd, illogical action to perform "in" a notebook.

• Option 2: "visualising" means forming a mental image of something — this is an internal mental process, not an action one does physically "in" a notebook.

• Option 3: "reading" is plausible on the surface (one can read a notebook), but the narrator is in the middle of an interview-day account, actively documenting her own thoughts/experience as she eats — "writing" fits the diary-like, first-person journalling context far better than "reading" something already written.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check for parallel grammatical structure (matching tense/form) between the blank and a nearby verb joined by "and"/"or".

• A "Moleskine notebook" is a well-known brand of notebook often associated with writers, journalists, and artists for jotting notes, sketches, or journal entries — a strong contextual clue pointing to "writing".
